newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW - Cumnock wants to survive.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW - Cumnock wants to survive.

text.p: Cumnock Coal Ltd, the subject of takeover speculation twice this year, said it needed higher production to ensure that it survived as a listed company.

Chairman Stanley Howard told Reuters the 1995/96 annual production rate of two million tonnes of coking and thermal coal from its Hunter Valley operations was not enough to guarantee survival in an industry undergoing constant rationalisation.
Cumnock fended off a hostile bid by Swiss commodities house Glencore Ag in early 1996 and until recently had been probed by CIM Resources Ltd as a potential merger partner.
Glencore's bid ended with a 25.14 percent stake and a pledge that it was a long term shareholder.

CIM, a neighbour of Cumnock in the Hunter Valley north of Sydney, has a five percent holding and at one time was keen on merging the two operations. But annoyed with Glencore's attitude, CIM said two months ago it was no longer interested.

Cumnock has an international share register, with Japanese and Chinese investors holding about 30 percent while a little-known Monaco-based investment group called Dafen Ltd acquired a 9.6 percent holding earlier this month after buying shares from former chairman and managing director Tom Johnson.

Howard, a former partner with large Sydney law firm Mallesons Stephen Jaques, became chairman last month after spending less than a year as the alternate director representing 11.2 percent shareholder Shenzen Energy Corp.
He said the initial priorities were to stabilise the board and appoint a new managing director.
After that, the company would look at increasing production.
"We are still in the transition stage of putting new management, and a new board, in place. It will all be part of the work to be done towards the end of this year and early next year."
Howard said Cumnock could increase production a number of ways, including expansion into an adjoining lease which it won by tender earlier this year and contained an estimated 270 million tonnes.
Although at an early stage of examination, this lease could be mined in two to three years. "We could either develop that way or acquire existing production," he said.

"I think we share the view that the other smaller coal companies have, that to deal effectively you need size," he said. "We are, in terms of production, about two million tonnes a year, and that is clearly not enough."
"Other companies feel the same way. I think there will be quite a bit of rationalisation in the industry," Howard said.

Cumnock produced a record 1.8 million tonnes in the year to June 30, well shy of its 2.2 million tonne target. But productivity gains allowed the company to boost output in the 1996/97 first quarter to an annual rate of 3.01 million tonnes.

Despite the improvement, brokers view Cumnock as a takeover stock and it is this rather than production increases which drive the share price. Glencore's A$2.50 offer price appeared attractive soon after its bid lapsed, with the stock slumping to a A$1.60 low when CIM said it had lost interest in a merger.
Dafen paid A$2.40 for its shares, which makes it the fourth largest shareholder behind Glencore, Itochu Corp of Japan with 19.97 percent and Shenzen.
Howard said he did not know much about Dafen or what their intentions were towards Cumnock.
"I suppose everybody is a target but I know of no particular moves (on Cumnock) at the moment."
Cumnock shares last traded on Tuesday at A$2.30, valuing the company at A$72.03 million based on 31.32 million shares on issue.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
